parts:
Hi all,

I am hoping for some help with a multistate Jolly-Seber model that I am trying to get running in Nimble. It seems as though Nimble is not respecting the state transitions. There are 6 states total and you can't move backwards. When I simulate from the model, there are individuals who are put in state 6 and then move into state 5 later (which is supposed to be impossible). I'm not sure what I am doing wrong. This model works in JAGS but I haven't managed to work out how to get it to work in Nimble.  I've attached the R code as well as the data if that is helpful. Any help you could provide would be very appreciated :) Thanks! 

############# MODEL ###############

## Constant adult phi and p
## 6 states total (3 juvenile states)

nimble_mod <- nimbleCode({
    
    #### Priors and Constraints ####
    
      # Dirichlet Prior for entry removal probabilities
      # for removal entry probabilities
      for(j in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
        for(i in 1:3){
          temp[j,i] ~ dgamma(1,1)
        }
          gamma_Matrix[j,1:3] <- temp[j,1:3]/sum(temp[j,1:3])
      }
        
      # Prior for constant adult survival
      phi ~ dbeta(1,1)
      
      # Prior for constant juvenile survival
      for(i in 1:3){
        phi_juv[i] ~ dbeta(1,1)      
      }
      # Prior for constant adult capture
    
      p ~ dbeta(1,1)   
      
      # Prior for constant juvenile capture
      for(i in 1:3){
        p_juv[i] ~ dbeta(1,1)  
      }
  
      for(j in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
        pstate[1,1,j] <- gamma_Matrix[j,1]
        pstate[1,2,j] <- gamma_Matrix[j,2]
        pstate[1,3,j] <- 0
        pstate[1,4,j] <- 0
        pstate[1,5,j] <- gamma_Matrix[j,3]
        pstate[1,6,j] <- 0
        
        pstate[2,1,j] <- 0
        pstate[2,2,j] <- 0
        pstate[2,3,j] <- phi_juv[1]
        pstate[2,4,j] <- 0
        pstate[2,5,j] <- 0
        pstate[2,6,j] <- (1-phi_juv[1])
        
        pstate[3,1,j] <- 0
        pstate[3,2,j] <- 0
        pstate[3,3,j] <- 0
        pstate[3,4,j] <- phi_juv[2]
        pstate[3,5,j] <- 0
        pstate[3,6,j] <- (1 - phi_juv[2])
        
        pstate[4,1,j] <- 0
        pstate[4,2,j] <- 0
        pstate[4,3,j] <- 0
        pstate[4,4,j] <- 0
        pstate[4,5,j] <- phi_juv[3]
        pstate[4,6,j] <- (1-phi_juv[3])
        
        pstate[5,1,j] <- 0
        pstate[5,2,j] <- 0
        pstate[5,3,j] <- 0
        pstate[5,4,j] <- 0
        pstate[5,5,j] <- phi
        pstate[5,6,j] <- (1-phi)
        
        pstate[6,1,j] <- 0
        pstate[6,2,j] <- 0
        pstate[6,3,j] <- 0
        pstate[6,4,j] <- 0
        pstate[6,5,j] <- 0
        pstate[6,6,j] <- 1
# Define probabilities of ind. i being observed at time j given S(j)
        # pobs[1,j] <- 0
        # pobs[2,j] <- p_juv[1]
        # pobs[3,j] <- p_juv[2]
        # pobs[4,j] <- p_juv[3]
        # pobs[5,j] <- p
        # pobs[6,j] <- 0
      }

pobs[1,1:n.occasions] <- 0
pobs[2,1:n.occasions] <- p_juv[1]
pobs[3,1:n.occasions] <- p_juv[2]
pobs[4,1:n.occasions] <- p_juv[3]
pobs[5,1:n.occasions] <- p
pobs[6,1:n.occasions] <- 0

    #### Likelihood ####
    
    for(i in 1:M){
    
      # Dummy occasion 1 where everyone is in state 1 (not yet in population)
      state[i,1] <- 1
      
      for(j in 2:n.occasions){
        
        # state of individual i at time j given previous state
        state[i,j] ~ dcat(pstate[state[i,j-1],1:6,j-1])
        
        # observation of individual i at time j given current state
        X[i,j] ~ dbern(pobs[state[i,j],j])
        
      }
      
    }
    
    #### Derived Parameters ####
    
    for(i in 1:M){
      for(j in 2:n.occasions){
        whenAlive_adult[i,j-1] <-  (state[i,j] == 5)*1
      }
      alive_adult[i] <- sum(whenAlive_adult[i,1:(n.occasions-1)])
    }
    
    for(j in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
      N_adult[j] <- sum(whenAlive_adult[1:M,j]) 
    }
    
    for(i in 1:M){
      z_adult[i] <- 1-(alive_adult[i] == 0)*1
    }

    N_super_adult <- sum(z_adult[1:M])

})

#### Determine Known States ####

# For Juveniles, they are first observed in State 2 (right after birth)
# If they are observed on the subsequent occasion, then they are in state 3
# if they are observed 2 occasions after birth they are in state 4, 
# if they are observed 3 or more occasions after birth they are in state 5


known.states.juv <- function(juv.ch){
  state <- matrix(NA,nrow=nrow(juv.ch),ncol=ncol(juv.ch))
  for(i in 1:nrow(juv.ch)){
    fst <- min(which(juv.ch[i,]==1))
    lst <- max(which(juv.ch[i,]==1))
    # don't know their state after last observation
    state[i,lst:(ncol(juv.ch))] <- NA
    # in State 1 before first observation (we redefine fst as state 2 next)
    state[i,1:fst] <- 1
    # in State 2 on first observation
    state[i,fst] <- 2
    # cover states between first and last observation
    if((lst - fst) >= 3){
      state[i,fst+1] <- 3
      state[i,fst+2] <- 4
      state[i,(fst+3):lst] <- 5
    }
    if((lst-fst) == 2){
      state[i,fst+1] <- 3
      state[i,fst+2] <- 4
    }
    if((lst-fst) == 1){
      state[i,fst+1] <- 3
    }
    else{
      next
    }
  }
  return(state)
}


# For adult CH, we assume they are adults when they are first observed
# thus between the first and last observation, the state is 5, before that
# the state is unknown so NA
known.states.adult <- function(ad.ch){
  state <- matrix(NA,nrow=nrow(ad.ch),ncol=ncol(ad.ch))
  for(i in 1:nrow(ad.ch)){
    fst <- min(which(ad.ch[i,]==1))
    lst <- max(which(ad.ch[i,]==1))
    state[i,fst:lst] <- 5
  }
  return(state)
}

ad_state <- known.states.adult(AD_CH.du)

# Add dummy occasion to Juv_CH

juv_state <- known.states.juv(JV_CH.du)


# Combine the known state matrices together
known_states_du <- rbind(ad_state,juv_state)


# Combine the observations together with the dummy first occasion
# where no one is yet observed. 

Xobs.du <- rbind(AD_CH.du,JV_CH.du)



#### Initial States for the latent values of the state matrix
# Put NA wherever the state is known and 1's before the known 
# states. 

initial.states <- function(ch,n.ad) {
  init_st <- matrix(NA,nrow=nrow(ch),ncol=ncol(ch))
  for(i in 1:n.ad){
    fst <- min(which(ch[i,]==1))
    lst <- max(which(ch[i,]==1))
    init_st[i,1:fst] <- 1
    init_st[i,fst] <- NA
    init_st[i,lst:ncol(ch)] <- 6
    init_st[i,lst] <- NA
  }
  for(i in (n.ad+1):nrow(ch)){
    fst <- min(which(ch[i,]==1))
    lst <- max(which(ch[i,]==1))
    init_st[i,1:fst] <- NA
    init_st[i,lst:ncol(ch)] <- 6
    init_st[i,lst] <- NA
  }
  return(init_st)
}

init_state_du <- initial.states(Xobs.du,nrow(AD_CH.du))


# Augment the data
n.aug <- 200
X_aug <- rbind(Xobs.du, matrix(0,ncol=ncol(Xobs.du),nrow=n.aug))


# Augment Initial state matrix and known state matrix

                          matrix(NA,nrow=n.aug,
                                 ncol=ncol(known_states_du)))
init_states_aug <- rbind(init_state_du, 
                         matrix(1,nrow=n.aug,
                                ncol=ncol(init_state_du)))

# set the first column of init_states_aug and known_states_aug = NA

known_states_aug[,1] <- NA



# Bundle Data

                  state = known_states_aug)

n.occasions <- ncol(X_aug)

init_gamma <- function()
{
temp <- matrix(0, nrow = n.occasions-1, ncol = 3)
gamma_Matrix <- temp
for(j in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
for(i in 1:3){
  temp[j,i] <- rgamma(1,1,1)
}
gamma_Matrix[j,] <- temp[j,]/sum(temp[j,1:3])
    }
  return(gamma_Matrix)
}

#### INITIAL VALUES

# Bundle Initial Values

MSJS_inits <- function(){
  
  list(phi=runif(1,0,1),phi_juv = runif(3,0,1), 
       p = runif(1,0,1),p_juv=runif(3,0,1),
       state = init_states_aug,
   gamma_Matrix = init_gamma())
}


# Parameters to be monitored
MSJS_params <- c("phi","p","N_adult","N_super_adult","gamma_Matrix",
                 "phi_juv","p_juv")

# MCMC settings
ni <- 10000
nt <- 1
nb <- 1000
nc <- 1

# Run JAGS model
constants <- list(
M = nrow(X_aug),
n.occasions = ncol(X_aug))

data <- list(X = X_aug,
             state = known_states_aug)

Rmodel <- nimbleModel(nimble_mod, constants, data, inits = MSJS_inits())

Hi Brittany,

I discovered this morning that yours and another nimble-users post had been placed in my spam folder by Google.  Unbelievable, Google!

Thanks for the thorough and runnable code with data.

I'm not 100% sure I'm seeing how to reproduce your error.  The code runs for me and appears to give reasonable results.  But I think I see maybe what is the problem/confusion.  Here are a few things I looked at:

First step, not the problem: after you build the model (nimbleModel), Rmodel$calculate() returns NA.  This is not necessarily an error but indicates incomplete initialization, which may later be filled in manually or by the MCMC drawing from priors.
# I explored like this:
Rmodel$calculate() #NA
for(v in Rmodel$getVarNames())
  print(paste(v, Rmodel$calculate(v)))
for(node in Rmodel$expandNodeNames("state"))
  print(paste(node, Rmodel$calculate(node)))
Rmodel$gamma_Matrix
Rmodel$temp

What I see is that temp and gamma_Matrix are not initialized, so the transition probabilities are not there.  When I look at MSJS_inits(), it looks like you are trying to initialize gamma_Matrix, but it has all deterministic nodes.  inits should only be for stochastic nodes (temp in this case).  But this looks like a minor side issue, not the cause of whatever the problem is.

You have 
# Rmodel$simulate()
# Rmodel$calculate()
commented out like that, so at first I didn't run them.

Your message said you get a problem when you simulate, and this is the only simulate call in the code, and it is commented out, so I wasn't quite sure if this is what you meant.  (Sometimes people informally/confusingly say "simulate" when they mean "sample using MCMC", so I'm wondering if that's what you meant?). Later I came back and tried these lines.  The simulate call here *can* give you invalid states because it will simulate *only* the non-data nodes.  The first case where this becomes invalid that I see is in row 5 of states.  Actually I did it with the Cmodel after running the MCMC, so my code looks like this:

Cmodel$simulate()
Cmodel$state[5,] # This is  1 5 6 6 5 5 5 5 5 6

What has happened is that elements 2:4 of this row of state are drawn from their distributions (because they are not data, and the first element has been filled deterministically), then elements 5:9 were not simulated because they *are* labeled as data.  The simulate method just calculates (for deterministic nodes) and draws random numbers (for stochastic nodes) in the order given.  It does not do any automatic determination of validity or of probability of nodes that depend on a newly drawn value.  You can overwrite data nodes (if that's what you want) using includeData = TRUE in the simulate call.  But, if you want to respect the data nodes, I think you'll have to write something more careful to do so.  It looks like the initial values are valid, and the MCMC seemed to run ok for me using those.  If you start with invalid sequences of states, the MCMC may recover from them, and/or it might be messy.

You can look at the state of the compiled model after MCMC simply by inspecting it, e.g.

Cmcmc$state

Also I noticed you have a call to runMCMC and then a call to Cmcmc$run, so I skipped the former and used the latter.

I hope this helps.  Sorry for the delay (ok google, why did you do that?) and let us know if this gets you on track.

-Perry

                          matrix(NA,nrow=n.aug,
                                 ncol=ncol(known_states_du)))

                                ncol=ncol(init_state_du)))

# set the first column of init_states_aug and known_states_aug = NA
init_states_aug[,1] <- NA
known_states_aug[,1] <- NA



# Bundle Data
MSJS_data <- list(X = X_aug, M=nrow(X_aug),n.occasions = ncol(X_aug),
                  state = known_states_aug)

n.occasions <- ncol(X_aug)

init_gamma <- function()
{
temp <- matrix(0, nrow = n.occasions-1, ncol = 3)
gamma_Matrix <- temp
for(j in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
for(i in 1:3){
  temp[j,i] <- rgamma(1,1,1)
}
gamma_Matrix[j,] <- temp[j,]/sum(temp[j,1:3])
    }
  return(gamma_Matrix)
}
